choices.explanation: Putting voice and data on the same VLAN removes the broadcast-domain separation that is the main reason for a voice VLAN.

choices.text: Place the port in the native VLAN of the trunk so the PC frames are untagged at the upstream switch.
choices.explanation: Native VLAN behaviour applies to trunks, not the phone/PC daisy chain on an access port.

questions.tip: Consider how the phone passes the PC's frames downstream.
questions.explanation:
Access ports with both a data and voice VLAN are the standard way to support a phone with a daisy-chained PC.

**Why it works:** The phone tags its own frames into the voice VLAN, and the PC's frames travel untagged in the data VLAN, all on a single access port.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Full trunk: not how phones present their downstream PC port.
- Single combined VLAN: loses voice/data separation.
- Native VLAN reference: applies to trunk links, not this configuration.

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, configure switching technologies and features.
questions.question:
During a switch audit, an engineer notices that the trunk between the distribution and access switch shows untagged frames being placed into VLAN 1 at one end and VLAN 99 at the other. CDP logs are filling with native VLAN mismatch errors and a small amount of traffic is leaking between the two VLANs.

Which corrective action best resolves the mismatch?

choices.text: Set the native VLAN to the same VLAN ID on both ends of the trunk.
choices.explanation: The native VLAN must match on both ends or untagged frames are interpreted in different VLANs at each side.

choices.text: Disable `802.1Q` tagging on the trunk so all frames are untagged.
choices.explanation: Removing tagging eliminates trunking entirely and collapses every VLAN into one broadcast domain.

choices.text: Change one side to ISL encapsulation to silence the dot1Q warning.
choices.explanation: Mixing encapsulations breaks the trunk; the warning indicates configuration, not protocol, mismatch.

choices.text: Configure both ends with the same MTU so the native VLAN frames pass without fragmentation.
choices.explanation: MTU is unrelated to native VLAN handling and would not stop the mismatch warning.

questions.tip: Focus on which parameter controls untagged frame placement on a trunk.
questions.explanation:
The native VLAN defines which VLAN untagged frames belong to on a dot1Q trunk, and both ends must agree.

**Why it works:** With matching native VLANs, untagged frames are interpreted consistently and no traffic leaks between VLANs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disabling tagging: removes all VLAN separation.
- ISL encapsulation: not how dot1Q mismatch is fixed.
- MTU: unrelated to native VLAN handling.

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, configure switching technologies and features.
questions.question:
Following a storage migration, two ESXi hosts and a NAS appliance now exchange large block-replication payloads over a dedicated VLAN. The vendor recommends sending frames of 9000 bytes end to end to reduce per-packet overhead. The engineer enables this on the host NICs but throughput remains poor and packet captures show fragmentation.

Which switch-side change is required to support the design?

choices.text: Enable jumbo frame support by raising the MTU on the involved switch ports and uplinks to 9216.
choices.explanation: Every L2 hop in the path must accept the larger MTU or frames will be dropped or fragmented.

choices.text: Increase the spanning-tree forward-delay timer to give larger frames more time to forward.
choices.explanation: STP timers are unrelated to frame size handling on a switch port.

choices.text: Change the duplex to half on the storage uplinks to reduce collisions on jumbo traffic.
choices.explanation: Half duplex on modern switched ports is a misconfiguration and would degrade performance further.

choices.text: Move the storage VLAN to the native VLAN of the trunk so the frames are not tagged.
choices.explanation: Native VLAN placement does not change the MTU the switch enforces on the link.

questions.tip: Consider what the switch must permit for frames larger than 1500 bytes.
questions.explanation:
Jumbo frames require the MTU to be raised on every switch hop along the path.

**Why it works:** Only when each port can accept 9000+ byte frames will the end-to-end path avoid drops or fragmentation.

**Why the others don't work:**
- STP timer change: irrelevant to frame size handling.
- Half duplex: would harm throughput, not help.
- Native VLAN: tagging does not affect MTU enforcement.

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, configure switching technologies and features.
questions.question:
A junior technician cabled a spare access switch into the lab incorrectly, creating two parallel uplinks back to the same distribution switch. Within seconds, broadcast traffic spiked, the management session locked up, and MAC address flapping appeared in the logs.

Which switch feature is designed to prevent this kind of loop from forming?

choices.text: Spanning Tree Protocol, which blocks redundant paths to leave a single active topology.
choices.explanation: STP detects the loop and places one of the parallel links into a blocking state to break it.

choices.text: Link aggregation with LACP across the two uplinks to merge them into one logical link.
choices.explanation: LACP only works when both ends are explicitly configured as a port channel, which was not the case here.

choices.text: Storm control with a strict broadcast threshold to drop loop-generated traffic.
choices.explanation: Storm control limits broadcast bursts but does not break the underlying L2 loop.

choices.text: Port security, which limits each port to a single learned MAC address.
choices.explanation: Port security restricts MAC learning but does not address parallel-link loops.

questions.tip: Identify the protocol that prevents L2 loops in redundant switch topologies.
questions.explanation:
STP exists specifically to prevent broadcast storms and MAC flapping in redundant switch designs.

**Why it works:** STP elects a root bridge, calculates least-cost paths, and places redundant ports into a blocking state so only one active path exists between any two switches.

**Why the others don't work:**
- LACP: requires explicit configuration on both ends; not automatic.
- Storm control: mitigates symptoms but not the loop.
- Port security: addresses MAC limits, not loops.

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, configure switching technologies and features.
questions.question:
The data centre team is configuring a four-port link aggregation between an access switch and a server's bonded NICs to provide both bandwidth and redundancy. The server is set for active LACP and the engineer wants the aggregation to come up cleanly.

Which TWO configuration items must match across the four switch ports involved?

choices.text: Speed and duplex settings on all member ports.
choices.explanation: LACP requires identical speed and duplex on all bundled members; mismatches prevent the group from bundling.

choices.text: Allowed VLAN list and trunking mode on all member ports.
choices.explanation: Switch ports in the same channel group must share VLAN and trunk parameters or LACP will reject the bundle.

choices.text: Spanning-tree priority must differ on each member port.
choices.explanation: STP runs on the logical port channel, not the individual members, so this is not a requirement.

choices.text: Each port must be in a different VLAN to allow load balancing.
choices.explanation: Members must share VLAN configuration; differing VLANs would prevent bundling.

choices.text: Each port must be configured as a routed (no switchport) interface.
choices.explanation: Routed-mode L3 ports cannot bundle with L2 switchports in a standard L2 LACP group.

questions.tip: Consider what consistency LACP demands across bundled ports.
questions.explanation:
Successful LACP bundling depends on consistent L1/L2 parameters across members.

**Why it works:** All ports must agree on speed, duplex, VLAN membership, and trunking mode, otherwise LACP suspends the inconsistent members.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Differing STP priority: STP applies to the logical channel.
- Different VLANs per port: bundle requires identical VLAN config.
- Routed-mode members: not compatible with L2 switchport bundle.

skills: 2.2: Given a scenario, configure switching technologies and features.
questions.question: Match each switching concept to the description that best fits it.

choices.text: VLAN whose frames traverse a trunk without a tag
choices.explanation: Untagged frames on a trunk are placed into the native VLAN at the receiving switch.

choices.text: Logical L3 interface representing a VLAN on a multilayer switch
choices.explanation: An SVI gives a VLAN an IP address so the switch can route between VLANs.

choices.text: Four-byte field inserted into Ethernet frames carrying the VLAN ID
choices.explanation: The dot1Q tag carries the VLAN ID and priority bits across a trunk.

choices.text: Ethernet frame with a payload larger than the default 1500-byte MTU
choices.explanation: Jumbo frames typically carry up to 9000 bytes of payload and require end-to-end MTU support.

questions.tip: Differentiate frame format features from logical L3 features.
questions.explanation: Each item describes a distinct switching concept in VLAN handling, L3 services, and frame size.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, select and configure wireless devices and technologies.
questions.question:
The wireless team is surveying a multi-tenant office on the 2.4 GHz band. Co-channel interference is high because every neighbouring AP is on a different overlapping channel and clients are reporting slow throughput. The engineer wants to standardise the access points across the floor.

Which channel selection minimises overlap on the 2.4 GHz band in most regulatory domains?

choices.text: Use only channels 1, 6, and 11 across the deployment.
choices.explanation: Channels 1, 6, and 11 are the standard non-overlapping 20 MHz channels available in the 2.4 GHz band in most regions.

choices.text: Use channels 2, 5, and 8 to spread coverage evenly across the band.
choices.explanation: These channels overlap each other and would worsen interference rather than reduce it.

choices.text: Use 40 MHz channel bonding to provide more bandwidth per AP.
choices.explanation: Bonding on 2.4 GHz leaves no non-overlapping channels and is widely discouraged.

choices.text: Use channels 36, 40, and 44 for cleaner spectrum.
choices.explanation: Those channels are in the 5 GHz band and cannot be selected for a 2.4 GHz radio.

questions.tip: Recall which channel set provides no overlap in 2.4 GHz.
questions.explanation:
Channels 1, 6, and 11 are the canonical non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels.

**Why it works:** Each is 20 MHz wide and spaced far enough apart that adjacent APs do not bleed into each other's spectrum.

**Why the others don't work:**
- 2/5/8: overlap heavily with each other.
- 40 MHz bonding on 2.4 GHz: removes any non-overlap option.
- 36/40/44: belong to a different band entirely.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, select and configure wireless devices and technologies.
questions.question:
A coffee shop chain wants visitors to connect to free Wi-Fi only after accepting an acceptable use policy and entering an email address. Staff devices use a separate corporate SSID and are not affected. The wireless platform must intercept the first HTTP request and present the policy page.

Which feature should the guest SSID be configured with?

choices.text: A captive portal that redirects new clients to the acceptance page before granting internet access.
choices.explanation: Captive portals are the standard mechanism for AUP acceptance and lightweight guest registration.

choices.text: `WPA3`-Enterprise with `802.1X` to authenticate each guest against a RADIUS server.
choices.explanation: Enterprise authentication is for known users with credentials, not anonymous guests.

choices.text: A hidden SSID broadcasting only after the user enters the email address.
choices.explanation: Hiding the SSID does not enforce policy acceptance and provides no real security.

choices.text: MAC address filtering with a whitelist of phones registered at the counter.
choices.explanation: MAC filtering does not scale to walk-in guests and is trivially bypassed.

questions.tip: Identify the feature that intercepts the first web request.
questions.explanation:
Captive portals are designed to intercept new associations and present terms before allowing onward traffic.

**Why it works:** The wireless controller redirects HTTP/HTTPS to a portal page; once the user accepts, the client MAC is permitted onto the internet path.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `WPA3`-Enterprise: requires user credentials, not suited to anonymous guests.
- Hidden SSID: not a policy or auth mechanism.
- MAC filtering: impractical for transient visitors.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, select and configure wireless devices and technologies.
questions.question:
The warehouse manager wants to extend Wi-Fi coverage to a long, narrow aisle between two metal racking rows. Coverage from omnidirectional ceiling APs is patchy because the signal is absorbed by the racks. The engineer needs to focus signal down the aisle.

Which antenna type best fits this requirement?

choices.text: A directional antenna such as a Yagi or patch pointed down the aisle.
choices.explanation: Directional antennas concentrate RF energy in a narrow beam, ideal for long corridors and aisles.

choices.text: An omnidirectional dipole antenna mounted at the centre of the aisle.
choices.explanation: Omnidirectional radiation would again be absorbed by the racking on both sides; that is the original problem.

choices.text: A high-gain omnidirectional mast antenna mounted at the end of the aisle.
choices.explanation: High-gain omnis flatten the donut pattern but still radiate in all horizontal directions, not down a corridor.

choices.text: A mesh repeater with a built-in omni at the far end of the aisle.
choices.explanation: A mesh hop still depends on antenna selection; an omnidirectional element does not focus down the aisle.

questions.tip: Think about which radiation pattern shapes signal along a corridor.
questions.explanation:
Directional antennas focus RF energy in a narrow beam, perfect for aisles and long rooms.

**Why it works:** A Yagi or patch projects most of its energy in the desired direction, reducing wasted signal sideways into racks or walls.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Dipole/omni: radiates equally in all horizontal directions, the original failure mode.
- High-gain omni: still omnidirectional, just flatter.
- Mesh repeater with omni: the antenna pattern still matters.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, select and configure wireless devices and technologies.
questions.question:
While planning a new campus rollout, the engineer wants central configuration, RF planning, and seamless client roaming across hundreds of APs in dozens of buildings. The APs should not store local configuration and must fail gracefully if a controller becomes unreachable.

Which AP architecture should be selected?

choices.text: Lightweight APs managed by a wireless LAN controller using CAPWAP tunnels.
choices.explanation: Lightweight/controller-based deployments centralise configuration, RF management, and roaming policies.

choices.text: Autonomous APs each configured individually via the local web UI.
choices.explanation: Autonomous APs do not centralise configuration or RF planning and do not scale well across campuses.

choices.text: Mesh APs daisy-chained from a single root node at the data centre.
choices.explanation: Mesh is a topology, not a management model, and a campus design typically uses wired uplinks per AP.

choices.text: Ad hoc mode peer-to-peer associations between APs to share configuration.
choices.explanation: Ad hoc mode is a client-to-client topology unsuitable for managed infrastructure.

questions.tip: Identify the architecture purpose-built for centralised wireless management.
questions.explanation:
Lightweight APs paired with a wireless LAN controller provide central management at scale.

**Why it works:** APs tunnel control and (optionally) data traffic to the WLC, which handles configuration, RF, and roaming policies.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Autonomous APs: per-device config, poor scale.
- Mesh-only design: appropriate for hard-to-cable areas, not a management decision.
- Ad hoc: a client topology, not infrastructure.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, select and configure wireless devices and technologies.
questions.question:
The security team is hardening the corporate wireless network. They want strong per-user authentication, protection against offline dictionary attacks on captured handshakes, and support for the latest standards.

Which TWO settings should be applied to the corporate SSID?

choices.text: Enable `WPA3`-Enterprise on the SSID.
choices.explanation: `WPA3`-Enterprise provides strong cryptographic suites and per-user authentication against an identity store.

choices.text: Authenticate users via `802.1X` to a RADIUS server backed by the directory.
choices.explanation: `802.1X` delivers per-user authentication tied to corporate identities, replacing shared keys.

choices.text: Use a single `WPA2`-PSK shared with all staff via the staff handbook.
choices.explanation: PSKs are vulnerable to offline cracking and provide no per-user accountability.

choices.text: Disable SSID broadcast to keep the network invisible to attackers.
choices.explanation: Hidden SSIDs are easily discovered and do not contribute to authentication strength.

choices.text: Enable MAC address filtering on the controller for corporate laptops.
choices.explanation: MAC filtering is trivially bypassed and not a substitute for user authentication.

questions.tip: Think about how enterprise wireless ties authentication to user identity.
questions.explanation:
Strong corporate wireless combines `WPA3`-Enterprise encryption with `802.1X` identity authentication.

**Why it works:** Each user gets their own session keys, derived from credentials checked against the directory, and `WPA3` raises the cryptographic baseline.

**Why the others don't work:**
- `WPA2`-PSK: shared secret with no per-user accountability.
- Hidden SSID: cosmetic, not security.
- MAC filtering: easily spoofed.

skills: 2.3: Given a scenario, select and configure wireless devices and technologies.
questions.question: Match each wireless identifier or topology term to its description.

choices.text: Human-readable network name advertised by the access point
choices.explanation: The SSID is the printable network name that clients see in their list.

choices.text: MAC address of the radio interface that identifies a single AP cell
choices.explanation: The BSSID uniquely identifies the radio serving a basic service set.

choices.text: Logical name shared across multiple APs forming a single extended network
choices.explanation: An ESSID groups multiple BSSIDs under one logical service set.

choices.text: Topology where wireless clients associate through an access point to a wired network
choices.explanation: Infrastructure mode contrasts with ad hoc, where clients talk peer-to-peer.

questions.tip: Differentiate the radio identifier from the user-visible name.
questions.explanation: SSID, BSSID, and ESSID describe different layers of wireless naming, while infrastructure mode describes the operating topology.

skills: 2.4: Explain important factors of physical installations.
questions.question:
The facilities team is planning a new branch fit-out where horizontal cabling from every desk terminates at a single comms cabinet on each floor. From there, fibre uplinks return to the central comms room in the basement. The branch architect needs the correct terminology for the floor cabinets versus the basement room when documenting the design.

Which labelling is correct?

choices.text: The floor cabinets are IDFs and the basement room is the MDF.
choices.explanation: MDF is the central distribution point; IDFs aggregate horizontal cabling on each floor and uplink to the MDF.

choices.text: The floor cabinets are MDFs and the basement room is the IDF.
choices.explanation: MDF and IDF are reversed; there is only one MDF and it is the main central facility.

choices.text: Both cabinets are MDFs because each holds its own patch panel.
choices.explanation: Holding a patch panel does not promote a cabinet to MDF status; MDF refers to the main central distribution point.

choices.text: Both rooms are IDFs because they distribute cables to endpoints.
choices.explanation: There must be a central MDF from which IDFs branch out; calling both IDFs leaves no main facility.

questions.tip: Recall which letter stands for the main facility.
questions.explanation:
MDF is the main distribution frame; IDFs are intermediate frames that uplink to it.

**Why it works:** Horizontal runs typically terminate at floor IDFs which then aggregate via vertical risers or fibre back to the single MDF.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Reversed labels: contradicts the hierarchy.
- Both as MDFs: there is only one main facility.
- Both as IDFs: leaves no central distribution point.

skills: 2.4: Explain important factors of physical installations.
questions.question:
Following a recent brownout that took down an edge router for several minutes, the operations team wants to ensure that mains dips no longer cause outages and that critical gear can ride through long enough for a controlled shutdown or generator handoff. The room already has a transfer switch from a backup generator but nothing between the mains and the rack.

Which device should be added directly upstream of the rack equipment?

choices.text: An uninterruptible power supply sized for the connected load.
choices.explanation: A UPS rides through sags and short outages on its battery and protects against mains transients.

choices.text: A power distribution unit with metered outlets.
choices.explanation: A PDU distributes power but does not provide battery backup or conditioning.

choices.text: A surge-protected power strip rated for the inrush current.
choices.explanation: A surge strip absorbs spikes but does not provide ride-through during sags or outages.

choices.text: An isolation transformer to decouple the rack from building ground.
choices.explanation: Isolation transformers address ground loops, not power-loss ride-through.

questions.tip: Identify which device provides ride-through during a power dip.
questions.explanation:
A UPS is purpose-built to bridge short outages and clean up the AC waveform.

**Why it works:** The battery and inverter keep equipment powered while the generator transfer occurs or while administrators shut systems down gracefully.

**Why the others don't work:**
- PDU: distributes power but does not back it up.
- Surge strip: filters spikes only.
- Isolation transformer: addresses grounding, not ride-through.

skills: 2.4: Explain important factors of physical installations.
questions.question:
The data centre operations team has noticed inlet temperatures on top-of-rack switches climbing above the vendor's recommended 27 C in the hot aisle. The switches have rear-to-front airflow but were installed front-to-back, drawing hot exhaust from neighbouring devices into their own intakes.

Which corrective action best addresses the airflow issue?

choices.text: Replace the switch fan modules with port-side intake or reverse-airflow variants that match the cold-aisle orientation.
choices.explanation: Matching the switch airflow direction to the room's hot/cold aisle layout fixes the recirculation root cause.

choices.text: Increase the CRAC setpoint to lower the cold-aisle temperature by 5 C.
choices.explanation: Overcooling masks the symptom but wastes energy and does not stop hot air being drawn into the wrong side.

choices.text: Install blanking panels in unused rack spaces to slow airflow.
choices.explanation: Blanking panels are correct general practice but do not solve a switch installed backwards relative to its airflow.

choices.text: Add a humidifier to the room to improve heat conduction across the switch chassis.
choices.explanation: Humidity in this range has negligible effect on chassis cooling and is not the issue.

questions.tip: Focus on aligning the device's airflow direction with the room layout.
questions.explanation:
Hot-aisle/cold-aisle layouts require devices whose intakes face the cold aisle and exhausts face the hot aisle.

**Why it works:** Reversing or replacing the fan modules ensures the switch draws cold supply air, not its neighbour's exhaust.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Lowering the setpoint: brute-force fix that wastes energy.
- Blanking panels: useful, but address a different recirculation path.
- Humidifier: does not address airflow direction.

skills: 2.4: Explain important factors of physical installations.
questions.question:
While re-cabling a wiring closet, the technician wants every desk drop to be terminated once on a fixed panel inside the rack, with short, replaceable cables connecting that panel to the switch ports. The goal is to keep solid-core horizontal cabling stationary and allow switch moves without disturbing the riser.

Which component fulfils this role?

choices.text: A patch panel terminating the solid-core cabling on punch-down blocks.
choices.explanation: Patch panels are the standard fixed termination for horizontal cabling, allowing stranded patch leads to switch ports.

choices.text: A keystone faceplate mounted at the rear of the rack.
choices.explanation: Faceplates terminate the desk end of the cable, not the rack-side aggregation point.

choices.text: A media converter chassis connected to each switch port.
choices.explanation: Media converters change physical media types but do not provide a fixed termination point for many runs.

choices.text: A cable manager mounted directly above the switch.
choices.explanation: Cable managers organise patch leads; they do not terminate cabling.

questions.tip: Identify the rack-side termination point for horizontal cabling.
questions.explanation:
Patch panels accept solid-core horizontal cabling on the rear via punch-downs and present `RJ45` jacks on the front for short patch leads to the switch.

**Why it works:** This keeps stiff, brittle solid-core wire stationary while flexible patch leads handle the daily moves and changes.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Faceplate: belongs at the desk end.
- Media converter: changes media type, not the termination architecture.
- Cable manager: organises, does not terminate.

skills: 2.4: Explain important factors of physical installations.
questions.question:
The architect is finalising environmental controls for a small server room that will host a single 42U rack of network and compute gear. Risk assessments highlight equipment damage from both fire and condensation as primary concerns.

Which TWO environmental controls should be included in the design?

choices.text: A clean-agent fire suppression system that does not damage electronics on discharge.
choices.explanation: Clean-agent suppression (such as FM-200 or inert gas) protects equipment from fire without water damage.

choices.text: Humidity control that holds relative humidity within the recommended band to avoid condensation and static.
choices.explanation: Keeping humidity in range prevents both condensation on cold surfaces and electrostatic discharge from overly dry air.

choices.text: A standard overhead wet-pipe sprinkler directly above the rack.
choices.explanation: Wet-pipe sprinklers cause significant water damage to electronics and are usually inappropriate for server rooms.

choices.text: An open-air ventilation duct to the outside to balance air pressure.
choices.explanation: An open external duct bypasses environmental controls and introduces dust, humidity, and contaminants.

choices.text: A portable space heater on a thermostat to keep the room above 25 C overnight.
choices.explanation: Heating a server room above its operating range stresses equipment and contradicts cooling goals.

questions.tip: Pair the fire and moisture concerns with appropriate dedicated controls.
questions.explanation:
Server rooms need fire suppression that does not destroy equipment and humidity control within the recommended band.

**Why it works:** Clean-agent suppression extinguishes without water, and humidity control prevents both condensation and ESD.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Wet-pipe sprinklers: destructive to electronics.
- Open external duct: defeats the controlled environment.
- Space heater: works against cooling.

skills: 2.4: Explain important factors of physical installations.
questions.question: Match each rack or facility component to its primary purpose.

choices.text: Provides battery-backed power to ride through outages and clean up transients
choices.explanation: A UPS keeps gear running during short outages and conditions incoming AC.

choices.text: Distributes mains power from a single inlet to multiple rack outlets
choices.explanation: A PDU is essentially a high-quality rack-mount power strip, often with metering or switching.

choices.text: Terminates copper horizontal cabling on punch-down blocks at the rack
choices.explanation: Patch panels provide a fixed termination for solid-core copper runs.

choices.text: Houses fibre splices and presents LC or SC bulkhead couplers for cross-connects
choices.explanation: Fibre distribution panels protect splices and provide clean fibre termination points.

questions.tip: Distinguish power components from cabling components.
questions.explanation: Each component plays a distinct role in physical infrastructure, covering power conditioning, distribution, and termination of copper and fibre.

skills: 3.1: Explain the purpose of organizational processes and procedures.
questions.question:
During an office relocation, the network team must produce documentation that shows how the new switches will be physically mounted, including the U-position of each device, patch panels, and PDUs in cabinet B12. The facilities contractor needs this before installing the cabinets next week.

Which type of documentation should the team produce?

choices.text: A rack diagram showing each device's U-position, cabling pathways, and power distribution layout.
choices.explanation: Rack diagrams document the physical layout inside a cabinet, including U-positions, PDUs, and patch panels.

choices.text: A Layer 3 logical diagram showing routed subnets and gateway addresses between floors.
choices.explanation: Layer 3 diagrams document routing topology, not physical equipment placement in a cabinet.

choices.text: A wireless heat map identifying expected coverage zones across the new floor plan.
choices.explanation: Heat maps show RF coverage, which is unrelated to cabinet equipment placement.

choices.text: An IPAM export listing the subnets and DHCP scopes assigned to the relocated VLANs.
choices.explanation: IPAM tracks IP allocation, not physical positioning of devices in a rack.

questions.tip: Match the documentation type to the physical-vs-logical question being asked.
questions.explanation:
The contractor needs the physical placement of equipment inside the cabinet.

**Why it works:** Rack diagrams are purpose-built for documenting physical U-position, cabling, and power within a cabinet.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Layer 3 logical: shows routing, not physical placement.
- Wireless heat map: shows RF coverage, not cabinet content.
- IPAM export: tracks addresses, not hardware mounting.

skills: 3.1: Explain the purpose of organizational processes and procedures.
questions.question:
The operations team is reviewing a vendor notice stating that a core router model will no longer receive security patches after March next year, though replacement parts will still be sold for another twelve months. Leadership wants to understand what this milestone means for the patch pipeline.

Which life-cycle status does the March date represent?

choices.text: End-of-support (EOS), after which the vendor no longer issues software or security updates.
choices.explanation: EOS marks the point when the vendor stops providing patches and security fixes, even if hardware is still sold.

choices.text: End-of-life (EOL), meaning the device cannot be purchased new from the vendor or partners.
choices.explanation: EOL refers to sales withdrawal, not the patching cutoff being described here.

choices.text: Decommissioning, the formal removal of the asset from production inventory.
choices.explanation: Decommissioning is an internal action, not a vendor support milestone.

choices.text: Configuration drift, where production settings diverge from the documented baseline.
choices.explanation: Configuration drift is unrelated to vendor support cycles.

questions.tip: Distinguish between sale availability and update availability.
questions.explanation:
Loss of security patches is the defining feature of end-of-support.

**Why it works:** EOS is specifically the vendor cutoff for software and security updates.

**Why the others don't work:**
- EOL: refers to the product no longer being sold.
- Decommissioning: internal retirement, not a vendor date.
- Configuration drift: a state, not a life-cycle phase.

skills: 3.1: Explain the purpose of organizational processes and procedures.
questions.question:
Following a misconfigured firewall change that caused a thirty-minute outage, the manager has asked the team to ensure that future modifications are formally reviewed, approved, scheduled, and have a documented rollback plan before being implemented. The team currently makes changes via ad hoc tickets only.

Which process should the team adopt?

choices.text: A change management process that includes a request, review board approval, scheduled window, and rollback plan.
choices.explanation: Change management formalises submission, review, approval, scheduling, and back-out planning for modifications.

choices.text: A configuration baseline lock that prevents any device from accepting CLI commands during business hours.
choices.explanation: Locking CLI access does not provide structured review or rollback procedures.

choices.text: An asset inventory refresh aligning warranty and license records with deployed hardware.
choices.explanation: Asset inventory tracks ownership, not the review of proposed changes.

choices.text: An updated SLA with the firewall vendor specifying response times for outage incidents.
choices.explanation: SLAs cover support response, not internal change approval workflows.

questions.tip: Look for the process that governs how changes are reviewed before deployment.
questions.explanation:
Structured review, approval, scheduling, and rollback are the core elements of change management.

**Why it works:** Change management is the discipline that formalises proposed modifications end-to-end.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Configuration baseline lock: technical control, not a process.
- Asset inventory refresh: unrelated to approving changes.
- Updated SLA: governs vendor response, not internal workflow.

skills: 3.1: Explain the purpose of organizational processes and procedures.
questions.question:
A junior engineer is preparing to deploy thirty new access switches across branch offices. Their lead wants each switch to start with an identical, vetted, known-good configuration that includes management VLAN, SNMPv3 credentials, NTP servers, and AAA settings before any site-specific tuning.

Which configuration type should the lead provide?

choices.text: A golden configuration that serves as the vetted baseline template applied to every new switch.
choices.explanation: A golden (baseline) configuration is the approved, standardized starting point for new deployments.

choices.text: A backup configuration pulled from one of the production switches at the busiest branch.
choices.explanation: A production backup may include site-specific drift and is not a vetted baseline.

choices.text: A logical network diagram annotated with the planned management VLAN and SNMP servers.
choices.explanation: A diagram documents topology but is not an applied configuration.

choices.text: An IPAM record reserving the management IP for each new switch at every branch.
choices.explanation: IPAM reservations address IP assignment, not the device configuration template.

questions.tip: Think about the standardised template used as the starting point.
questions.explanation:
The vetted, identical baseline template is the golden configuration.

**Why it works:** Golden configurations are explicitly the approved baseline for new device rollouts.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Backup config: reflects production drift, not a baseline.
- Logical diagram: documentation, not configuration.
- IPAM record: covers addressing only.

skills: 3.1: Explain the purpose of organizational processes and procedures.
questions.question:
A new manager has inherited a network with sparse documentation and is establishing a documentation baseline. They want a record of which IP subnets, DHCP scopes, and reservations exist enterprise-wide, and a separate record showing every deployed hardware asset along with its serial number, warranty expiry, and software license.

Which TWO documentation artefacts should the manager prioritise to meet these two needs?

choices.text: An IP address management (IPAM) system tracking subnets, scopes, reservations, and utilisation.
choices.explanation: IPAM is the dedicated tool for documenting address space, scopes, and reservations.

choices.text: An asset inventory recording hardware, serial numbers, warranty support, and software licensing.
choices.explanation: Asset inventory captures hardware, license, and warranty data per the requirement.

choices.text: A site-wide wireless heat map showing predicted RF coverage in each building.
choices.explanation: Heat maps document RF coverage, not IP space or hardware inventory.

choices.text: A rack diagram for every cabinet with U-position labels and PDU layouts.
choices.explanation: Rack diagrams cover physical layout, not the requested IP or asset data.

choices.text: A service-level agreement template for hardware vendor response times.
choices.explanation: An SLA template governs vendor responses rather than internal documentation of assets and IPs.

questions.tip: Pair the artefact to the data each requirement names.
questions.explanation:
IPAM tracks address space; the asset inventory tracks hardware, licensing, and warranty data.

**Why it works:** Each tool maps directly to one of the two stated needs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Heat map: RF coverage only.
- Rack diagram: physical layout only.
- SLA template: vendor response governance.

skills: 3.1: Explain the purpose of organizational processes and procedures.
questions.question: Match each network documentation or process artefact to its primary purpose.

choices.text: Documents how cables physically connect devices, ports, and patch panels across the site
choices.explanation: Physical diagrams show actual cabling paths and port connections between equipment.

choices.text: Shows VLANs, subnets, routing relationships, and traffic flow without physical media detail
choices.explanation: Logical diagrams represent the abstract topology of networks and routing.

choices.text: Defines agreed availability, response, and resolution targets between a provider and customer
choices.explanation: SLAs are formal commitments about service quality between two parties.

choices.text: Visualises measured or predicted RF signal strength across a floor plan to plan AP placement
choices.explanation: Heat maps map RF coverage onto a floor plan to identify gaps and overlap.

questions.tip: Distinguish physical media from logical relationships and from service or RF artefacts.
questions.explanation: Each artefact has a distinct purpose: cabling, topology, contractual targets, or RF coverage.

skills: 3.2: Given a scenario, use network monitoring technologies.
questions.question:
The operations team is rolling out SNMP polling for a hundred core and distribution switches. Security has mandated that polling traffic must be authenticated and encrypted in transit, and that community-string-based authentication is no longer acceptable.

Which SNMP version should the team configure on the devices?

choices.text: SNMPv3 with authPriv mode for authenticated and encrypted polling.
choices.explanation: SNMPv3 supports user-based authentication and message encryption; authPriv provides both.

choices.text: SNMPv2c with a long, randomised community string sent over the management VLAN.
choices.explanation: SNMPv2c uses community strings sent in cleartext and does not encrypt traffic.

choices.text: SNMPv1 with read-only community strings only, restricted by ACL.
choices.explanation: SNMPv1 also uses cleartext community strings without authentication or encryption.

choices.text: SNMPv2c traps tunnelled through a syslog forwarder to the collector.
choices.explanation: Syslog tunnelling does not encrypt SNMP and is not a standard transport.

questions.tip: Identify which SNMP version provides both authentication and confidentiality.
questions.explanation:
Only SNMPv3 provides authenticated, encrypted polling.

**Why it works:** SNMPv3 authPriv combines user authentication with message encryption.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SNMPv2c: cleartext community strings.
- SNMPv1: cleartext community strings.
- SNMPv2c over syslog: invalid transport that does not encrypt SNMP payload.

skills: 3.2: Given a scenario, use network monitoring technologies.
questions.question:
The performance team needs to know which source and destination IPs, ports, and protocols are using the most bandwidth on the WAN edge over the past 24 hours, but they do not need full packet payloads. Storage on the collector is limited.

Which monitoring method should the team enable on the edge router?

choices.text: Flow data export such as NetFlow or IPFIX, summarising sources, destinations, ports, and byte counts per flow.
choices.explanation: Flow data summarises conversations without storing payloads, ideal for bandwidth analysis.

choices.text: Full packet capture mirrored to a sniffer on the WAN-facing interface.
choices.explanation: Full packet capture stores payloads and consumes disk quickly, exceeding the stated storage constraint.

choices.text: SNMP polling of interface counters every five minutes to derive top talkers.
choices.explanation: Interface counters give totals per interface, not per conversation or per port.

choices.text: Syslog forwarding of routing protocol events to a central collector.
choices.explanation: Syslog routing events do not include traffic conversation data.

questions.tip: Match the data type to what each method actually records.
questions.explanation:
Flow data is engineered for conversation-level reporting without payload overhead.

**Why it works:** NetFlow/IPFIX records source, destination, ports, and bytes per flow, which directly answers the question.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Full packet capture: stores payload, exceeds storage limit.
- SNMP interface counters: aggregate by interface, not by flow.
- Syslog of routing events: no traffic content.

skills: 3.2: Given a scenario, use network monitoring technologies.
questions.question:
An analyst needs to examine the full payload of suspicious DNS traffic transiting a core switch without disrupting production sessions. The switch will be configured to copy traffic from VLAN 30 to a dedicated sensor port where Wireshark runs.

Which switch feature should be configured?

choices.text: Port mirroring (SPAN) copying VLAN 30 traffic to the sensor interface.
choices.explanation: Port mirroring duplicates traffic to an analysis port without affecting forwarding.

choices.text: An SNMP trap receiver configured to forward DNS events to the sensor.
choices.explanation: SNMP traps do not carry packet payloads.

choices.text: Syslog forwarding from the switch to the sensor's UDP/514 listener.
choices.explanation: Syslog carries log messages, not the original DNS packets.

choices.text: An ACL on VLAN 30 that drops DNS responses to the sensor.
choices.explanation: Dropping traffic would prevent analysis and impact users.

questions.tip: Choose the feature that delivers raw packets to an analysis tool.
questions.explanation:
Port mirroring is the standard mechanism to copy live traffic to a packet analyser.

**Why it works:** SPAN/mirror copies frames to a target port for tools like Wireshark.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SNMP traps: event notifications only.
- Syslog: log messages, not packets.
- ACL drop: blocks traffic, defeating the goal.

skills: 3.2: Given a scenario, use network monitoring technologies.
questions.question:
After a week of capturing performance data from every core switch, the team wants the monitoring platform to alert when CPU, interface utilisation, or memory deviate significantly from typical patterns observed during normal operations.

Which monitoring concept should the team configure?

choices.text: Baseline metrics with anomaly-based alerting thresholds tied to deviations from normal patterns.
choices.explanation: Baselines define normal, and anomaly alerts trigger on statistically significant deviations.

choices.text: Static SNMP trap thresholds set to the device vendor's recommended ceilings.
choices.explanation: Static vendor ceilings do not adapt to each environment's normal pattern.

choices.text: Full packet capture on every uplink for retrospective deep analysis.
choices.explanation: Capture provides forensic data, not proactive deviation alerts.

choices.text: Scheduled network discovery sweeps to refresh the device inventory daily.
choices.explanation: Discovery finds devices; it does not detect performance anomalies.

questions.tip: Identify the technique that compares current behaviour against a learned normal.
questions.explanation:
Baseline-driven anomaly alerting is the textbook approach.

**Why it works:** Baselines establish normal; deviations trigger alerts.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Static vendor thresholds: ignore site-specific norms.
- Packet capture: forensic, not proactive.
- Discovery: inventory only.

skills: 3.2: Given a scenario, use network monitoring technologies.
questions.question:
The security team wants every switch, router, and firewall log to land in a single platform where events from different vendors can be correlated, searched, and used to drive alerting against playbooks. Today, each device writes to its own local buffer.

Which TWO components should the team deploy to meet this requirement?

choices.text: A syslog collector receiving log messages forwarded from every network device.
choices.explanation: A syslog collector centralises log forwarding from heterogeneous devices.

choices.text: A SIEM platform that ingests, parses, correlates, and alerts on aggregated log data.
choices.explanation: A SIEM provides cross-vendor correlation, search, and playbook alerting on collected logs.

choices.text: A scheduled network discovery sweep producing a fresh device inventory each night.
choices.explanation: Discovery enumerates devices but does not aggregate or correlate logs.

choices.text: A NetFlow exporter sampling 1-in-100 packets at each edge router.
choices.explanation: Flow data covers conversations, not vendor log messages.

choices.text: An SNMP trap receiver collecting interface state changes from every device.
choices.explanation: Trap receivers handle SNMP-specific events, not full vendor logs or correlation.

questions.tip: Two complementary tools are needed for centralisation and for correlation.
questions.explanation:
A syslog collector centralises the messages; the SIEM correlates and alerts on them.

**Why it works:** Syslog collection + SIEM is the standard log aggregation pattern.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Discovery: inventory only.
- NetFlow: flow data, not logs.
- SNMP traps: limited scope, no correlation.

skills: 3.2: Given a scenario, use network monitoring technologies.
questions.question: Match each monitoring solution category to the question it is best suited to answer.

choices.text: How are CPU, memory, latency, and interface utilisation trending against the baseline
choices.explanation: Performance monitoring tracks resource and throughput metrics over time.

choices.text: Is each device reachable and responding to health checks right now
choices.explanation: Availability monitoring focuses on up/down state and reachability.

choices.text: Has any device's running configuration changed compared to the approved version
choices.explanation: Configuration monitoring detects drift against an approved baseline or golden config.

choices.text: Which applications, sources, and destinations consume the most bandwidth on the WAN
choices.explanation: Traffic analysis uses flow or capture data to attribute consumption by conversation.

questions.tip: Think about whether each tool asks about state, health, drift, or usage.
questions.explanation: Each solution category answers a distinct operational question.

skills: 3.3: Explain disaster recovery (DR) concepts.
questions.question:
During a DR planning workshop, the business owner states that the order entry system can lose no more than fifteen minutes of transaction data in the event of a major failure. The architect needs to translate this into a measurable DR metric for the replication design.

Which DR metric does this fifteen-minute limit represent?

choices.text: Recovery point objective (RPO), the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
choices.explanation: RPO defines the maximum data loss tolerated, expressed as a time interval since the last good copy.

choices.text: Recovery time objective (RTO), the maximum acceptable time to restore service.
choices.explanation: RTO measures restoration time, not how much data may be lost.

choices.text: Mean time to repair (MTTR), the average time taken to fix a failed component.
choices.explanation: MTTR is a historical maintenance average, not a planning target for data loss.

choices.text: Mean time between failures (MTBF), the average operational interval between failures.
choices.explanation: MTBF measures reliability, not data-loss tolerance.

questions.tip: Distinguish data-loss limits from time-to-restore limits.
questions.explanation:
Data-loss tolerance is expressed by RPO.

**Why it works:** RPO sets how stale the recovered data may be, which is exactly what the business owner stated.

**Why the others don't work:**
- RTO: time to restore service.
- MTTR: historic repair average.
- MTBF: reliability metric.

skills: 3.3: Explain disaster recovery (DR) concepts.
questions.question:
The operations team has been asked to provide a DR facility that can take over production within minutes of a primary site failure, with replicated data and running services already in place. Budget has been approved for this most expensive option.

Which type of DR site meets the requirement?

choices.text: A hot site with replicated data and running infrastructure ready to assume production traffic.
choices.explanation: Hot sites mirror production and can fail over within minutes.

choices.text: A warm site stocked with hardware and network connectivity but requiring data restore and service start-up.
choices.explanation: Warm sites need significant restore time before they can take production.

choices.text: A cold site providing only space, power, and cooling, with hardware shipped in during an event.
choices.explanation: Cold sites take days or longer to bring online and do not meet a minutes-level target.

choices.text: A tabletop facility used for periodic DR exercises and validation tests.
choices.explanation: Tabletop is an exercise type, not a DR site classification.

questions.tip: Match the readiness state of each site to the time needed for cutover.
questions.explanation:
Only a hot site provides the near-immediate cutover described.

**Why it works:** Hot sites carry live replicated state and running services.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Warm: needs restore and start-up time.
- Cold: only physical facility, no equipment ready.
- Tabletop: an exercise format, not a site.

skills: 3.3: Explain disaster recovery (DR) concepts.
questions.question:
An e-commerce platform has two firewalls deployed at the perimeter. Both forward production traffic concurrently, share session state, and each carries roughly half the load during normal operations. If one fails, the surviving unit absorbs the full load.

Which high-availability approach is in use?

choices.text: Active-active, where both nodes simultaneously serve production and share state.
choices.explanation: Active-active runs both nodes in production, distributing load and sharing session state.

choices.text: Active-passive, where the secondary node remains idle until the primary fails.
choices.explanation: In active-passive, only the primary serves traffic until failover, which contradicts the scenario.

choices.text: Cold standby, where the secondary node is powered off and brought online manually after a failure.
choices.explanation: Cold standby is not part of the active-active or active-passive pair concept.

choices.text: Tabletop redundancy, a walk-through review of failover procedures with no live nodes.
choices.explanation: Tabletop is a DR exercise format, not a deployment topology.

questions.tip: Look at whether both nodes serve traffic simultaneously.
questions.explanation:
Concurrent load sharing with state sync is active-active.

**Why it works:** Both nodes participate in production simultaneously.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Active-passive: secondary idle.
- Cold standby: powered-off secondary.
- Tabletop: an exercise, not a topology.

skills: 3.3: Explain disaster recovery (DR) concepts.
questions.question:
The IT director wants the DR team to walk through the failover playbook for the ERP system in a conference room, discussing decisions, communications, and handoffs without actually moving production workloads or interrupting services. Each role-holder should narrate what they would do.

Which type of DR exercise should be scheduled?

choices.text: A tabletop exercise where participants discuss the response without enacting it on production systems.
choices.explanation: Tabletop exercises walk through scenarios verbally, with no production impact.

choices.text: A full failover validation test that cuts production traffic to the DR site and back.
choices.explanation: Full failover validation actually moves workloads, which contradicts the constraint.

choices.text: A simulated DDoS drill against the production load balancer to test resilience.
choices.explanation: A DDoS drill is a security exercise, not a DR walk-through.

choices.text: A change advisory board meeting to approve the new ERP release window.
choices.explanation: A CAB review approves changes; it is not a DR exercise.

questions.tip: Identify the exercise type that uses discussion rather than action.
questions.explanation:
A discussion-based, non-disruptive review is a tabletop exercise.

**Why it works:** Tabletop exercises are designed for narrative walk-through.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Full failover: actually moves production.
- DDoS drill: a different test type.
- CAB meeting: change governance, not DR.

skills: 3.3: Explain disaster recovery (DR) concepts.
questions.question:
A finance application currently has an RTO of eight hours and an RPO of four hours, both of which leadership now considers too long. The business has approved investment in shorter recovery objectives. The architect is considering options that reduce data loss and reduce service downtime simultaneously.

Which TWO design changes most directly improve these two metrics?

choices.text: Increase replication frequency between sites so the secondary copy is closer to real-time.
choices.explanation: Tighter replication reduces the data gap and improves RPO.

choices.text: Pre-stage running infrastructure at a hot site so cutover takes minutes rather than hours.
choices.explanation: Pre-started infrastructure reduces recovery time, improving RTO.

choices.text: Lengthen the backup retention window to keep more historical restore points.
choices.explanation: Retention affects history available, not RPO or RTO improvements.

choices.text: Add a tabletop exercise schedule to validate the documentation annually.
choices.explanation: Tabletop exercises validate plans but do not shorten RPO or RTO.

choices.text: Move to a cold site with shipped-in hardware to lower facility cost.
choices.explanation: Cold sites worsen RTO, not improve it.

questions.tip: Pair each metric with the design change that directly reduces it.
questions.explanation:
Tighter replication cuts RPO; a ready hot site cuts RTO.

**Why it works:** Each chosen change addresses one metric directly.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Longer retention: history, not recovery objectives.
- Tabletop: validation only.
- Cold site: worsens RTO.

skills: 3.3: Explain disaster recovery (DR) concepts.
questions.question: Match each DR metric to its definition.

choices.text: Maximum amount of data, measured in time, that the business can lose during a disaster
choices.explanation: RPO defines tolerated data loss as a time interval.

choices.text: Maximum time the business can be without the service before unacceptable impact
choices.explanation: RTO is the time to restore service after disruption.

choices.text: Average time taken to restore a failed component once a fault is detected
choices.explanation: MTTR is the maintenance/repair average.

choices.text: Average operational time between failures of a component during normal use
choices.explanation: MTBF is a reliability metric averaged across observed failures.

questions.tip: Distinguish planning targets (RPO, RTO) from reliability measurements (MTTR, MTBF).
questions.explanation: RPO and RTO are forward-looking targets; MTTR and MTBF are reliability statistics.

skills: 3.4: Given a scenario, implement IPv4 and IPv6 network services.
questions.question:
Branch office clients are on VLAN 40 (10.40.0.0/24) but the DHCP server lives in the data centre on a different subnet. Clients are receiving APIPA addresses because their DHCPDISCOVER broadcasts are not reaching the central server. The router for VLAN 40 has no DHCP relay configured.

Which configuration should be applied to the VLAN 40 gateway interface?

choices.text: Configure a DHCP relay (IP helper-address) pointing to the central DHCP server.
choices.explanation: DHCP relay forwards broadcast DISCOVER messages as unicast to a remote DHCP server.

choices.text: Shorten the DHCP lease time on the central server to one hour.
choices.explanation: Lease length does not address the broadcast-domain boundary.

choices.text: Add a DHCP exclusion range for the branch subnet on the central server.
choices.explanation: Exclusions reserve addresses; they do not deliver DISCOVERs across subnets.

choices.text: Enable SLAAC on the VLAN 40 interface so clients self-configure addresses.
choices.explanation: SLAAC is an IPv6 mechanism and does not provide IPv4 leases.

questions.tip: Identify the feature that crosses a broadcast boundary for DHCP.
questions.explanation:
A DHCP relay/IP helper forwards client broadcasts across subnets.

**Why it works:** Relay converts the broadcast DISCOVER into unicast toward the configured server.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Lease time: unrelated to delivery.
- Exclusion: address management on the server.
- SLAAC: IPv6 only.

skills: 3.4: Given a scenario, implement IPv4 and IPv6 network services.
questions.question:
The mail administrator has migrated the company's inbound email service to a new provider. Outbound delivery from external senders is now bouncing because remote mail servers are not finding the new provider when looking up the company domain.

Which DNS record type must be updated to direct inbound mail to the new provider?

choices.text: MX records pointing to the new mail provider's hostnames with appropriate priorities.
choices.explanation: MX records publish the mail exchangers for a domain, used by sending servers.

choices.text: TXT records containing the new provider's SPF authorisation string.
choices.explanation: SPF authorises senders but does not direct inbound mail routing.

choices.text: `PTR` records associating the new provider's IPs with the company hostname.
choices.explanation: `PTR` records support reverse DNS, not mail routing.

choices.text: `CNAME` records aliasing the company domain apex to the provider's hostname.
choices.explanation: A domain apex generally cannot host a `CNAME`, and CNAMEs do not advertise mail routing.

questions.tip: Identify the record type that publishes mail exchangers.
questions.explanation:
MX records are the standard mechanism for advertising inbound mail servers.

**Why it works:** Sending MTAs look up MX records to choose where to deliver mail.

**Why the others don't work:**
- TXT/SPF: authorisation only.
- `PTR`: reverse DNS.
- `CNAME` at apex: not valid and not used for routing.

skills: 3.4: Given a scenario, implement IPv4 and IPv6 network services.
questions.question:
Security has reported that internal users could be vulnerable to cache poisoning, where a resolver might accept forged responses claiming to be authoritative for a public banking domain. They want resolvers to cryptographically validate that responses come from the legitimate zone owner.

Which DNS feature should be implemented?

choices.text: DNSSEC validation on resolvers to cryptographically verify response authenticity.
choices.explanation: DNSSEC signs records and lets resolvers validate the chain of trust.

choices.text: Switch all resolvers to a primary forward-only configuration to a single ISP DNS.
choices.explanation: Forwarding alone does not authenticate responses cryptographically.

choices.text: Add a long TTL to all A records so cache entries do not refresh as often.
choices.explanation: Longer TTLs increase exposure to poisoned entries rather than reducing it.

choices.text: Disable recursion on internal resolvers to limit query scope.
choices.explanation: Disabling recursion breaks normal resolution and does not validate responses.

questions.tip: Look for the mechanism that adds cryptographic validation to DNS.
questions.explanation:
DNSSEC provides record signing and chain-of-trust validation.

**Why it works:** Resolvers can verify each answer's signature against published keys.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Forwarding only: no authentication.
- Long TTLs: extend exposure.
- Disable recursion: breaks resolution.

skills: 3.4: Given a scenario, implement IPv4 and IPv6 network services.
questions.question:
An engineer is enabling IPv6 on a guest VLAN where there is no DHCPv6 server. The router will advertise the /64 prefix on the segment, and clients should derive their own host addresses without contacting a central server.

Which address-configuration method is in use?

choices.text: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) using router-advertised prefixes.
choices.explanation: SLAAC derives host addresses from RA-advertised prefixes without a DHCP server.

choices.text: DHCPv6 relay forwarding solicits to the central DHCPv6 server.
choices.explanation: No DHCPv6 server exists, so a relay would have nothing to forward to.

choices.text: IPv4 DHCP reservations mapped to client MAC addresses.
choices.explanation: DHCP reservations apply to IPv4, not IPv6 autoconfiguration.

choices.text: Static IPv6 addressing manually configured per client.
choices.explanation: Static configuration contradicts the requirement for self-derived addresses.

questions.tip: Identify which IPv6 mechanism does not require a DHCP server.
questions.explanation:
SLAAC relies only on router advertisements for prefix information.

**Why it works:** Clients combine the advertised /64 with an interface identifier.

**Why the others don't work:**
- DHCPv6 relay: no server available.
- IPv4 reservations: wrong protocol.
- Static: not self-derived.

skills: 3.4: Given a scenario, implement IPv4 and IPv6 network services.
questions.question:
An ISP is rolling out encrypted DNS to its customer base to prevent third parties on the path from observing or modifying DNS queries. The team has been asked to support the two industry-standard transports for encrypting DNS between client and resolver.

Which TWO protocols should the ISP support?

choices.text: DNS over TLS (DoT), encrypting DNS traffic typically on TCP/853.
choices.explanation: DoT wraps DNS in TLS over its own dedicated port.

choices.text: DNS over HTTPS (DoH), encrypting DNS queries inside HTTPS sessions.
choices.explanation: DoH tunnels DNS over standard HTTPS, blending with web traffic.

choices.text: DNSSEC validation on stub resolvers for chain-of-trust verification.
choices.explanation: DNSSEC provides authenticity but not transport confidentiality.

choices.text: DNS over UDP/53 with extended record types for response signing.
choices.explanation: Plain UDP/53 is unencrypted by definition.

choices.text: Recursive forwarding to a public resolver over IPsec site-to-site tunnels.
choices.explanation: Site-to-site IPsec is not a standard DNS transport for end clients.

questions.tip: Both correct answers are dedicated encrypted DNS transports.
questions.explanation:
DoT and DoH are the two recognised encrypted DNS transports.

**Why it works:** Each is purpose-built for confidential client-to-resolver DNS.

**Why the others don't work:**
- DNSSEC: authenticity, not encryption.
- UDP/53: unencrypted.
- IPsec tunnels: not a client-side DNS transport.

skills: 3.4: Given a scenario, implement IPv4 and IPv6 network services.
questions.question: Match each DNS record type to the resolution task it supports.

choices.text: Maps a hostname to an IPv4 address
choices.explanation: A records resolve a name to a 32-bit IPv4 address.

choices.text: Maps a hostname to an IPv6 address
choices.explanation: `AAAA` records resolve a name to a 128-bit IPv6 address.

choices.text: Aliases one hostname to another canonical hostname
choices.explanation: `CNAME` records create a name alias pointing to another name.

choices.text: Maps an IP address back to a hostname for reverse lookups
choices.explanation: `PTR` records are used in reverse DNS zones.

choices.text: Identifies the authoritative name servers for a zone
choices.explanation: NS records delegate or identify authoritative servers for a domain.

questions.tip: Distinguish forward vs reverse mapping and aliasing vs delegation.
questions.explanation: Each record type fills a distinct DNS role: forward IPv4, forward IPv6, aliasing, reverse, and delegation.

skills: 3.5: Compare and contrast network access and management methods.
questions.question:
Two regional offices need their internal subnets to communicate as if they were on the same private network, with the tunnel established between the firewalls at each location and remaining up at all times. Individual user devices should require no VPN client.

Which VPN topology meets this requirement?

choices.text: A site-to-site VPN between the office firewalls, providing always-on tunnel between subnets.
choices.explanation: Site-to-site VPNs interconnect networks at the gateway level without per-user clients.

choices.text: A client-to-site VPN with full tunnel configured on every endpoint at both offices.
choices.explanation: Client-to-site requires endpoint software and does not interconnect subnets at the gateway.

choices.text: A clientless SSL VPN portal published at each office for users to browse to.
choices.explanation: Clientless VPNs publish individual applications, not subnet-level routing.

choices.text: A jump box at one site that users at the other site connect to over SSH.
choices.explanation: A jump box provides administrative access, not subnet interconnection.

questions.tip: Identify the VPN topology that connects networks rather than individual users.
questions.explanation:
Gateway-to-gateway interconnect is the textbook site-to-site model.

**Why it works:** Firewalls at each site form the tunnel; clients need no software.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Client-to-site: per-user model.
- Clientless portal: application-level access.
- Jump box: admin access only.

skills: 3.5: Compare and contrast network access and management methods.
questions.question:
A remote worker connects to corporate via a client-to-site VPN. The security team requires that all of the worker's traffic, including browsing the public internet, traverse the VPN so that corporate web filtering and inspection apply uniformly. Local internet break-out is not acceptable.

Which tunnel mode should be configured?

choices.text: Full tunnel, where all client traffic is sent through the VPN to corporate.
choices.explanation: Full tunnel routes every flow through the VPN, enabling corporate inspection of all traffic.

choices.text: Split tunnel, where only corporate destinations traverse the VPN.
choices.explanation: Split tunnel allows local internet break-out, which the policy prohibits.

choices.text: Clientless SSL VPN, where users access only published web apps.
choices.explanation: Clientless does not route arbitrary traffic, so public browsing would be unaffected.

choices.text: Out-of-band management over a dedicated cellular link.
choices.explanation: Out-of-band management is not a VPN tunnel mode for end users.

questions.tip: Match the routing scope of each mode to the inspection requirement.
questions.explanation:
Inspecting all traffic requires full tunnel.

**Why it works:** Full tunnel forces every flow through corporate.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Split tunnel: allows local egress.
- Clientless: no general traffic routing.
- OOB management: unrelated.

skills: 3.5: Compare and contrast network access and management methods.
questions.question:
Administrators need to manage core routers even when the production data plane is fully congested or the routing protocol has collapsed. The proposed design provisions a separate cellular-attached console server reachable only by the management team.

Which management approach is being described?

choices.text: Out-of-band management, using a dedicated path independent of the production data plane.
choices.explanation: OOB management uses a separate path so admins can reach devices when production is down.

choices.text: In-band management using SSH over the production management VLAN.
choices.explanation: In-band shares the same data plane that is congested or down.

choices.text: Clientless VPN access through the production firewall to the management subnet.
choices.explanation: This still depends on the production path being available.

choices.text: A jump box reachable only through the production VPN concentrator.
choices.explanation: A jump box on the production path provides no resilience if that path fails.

questions.tip: Look for the approach that survives a production data-plane outage.
questions.explanation:
A separate cellular path is the defining feature of out-of-band management.

**Why it works:** OOB keeps an alternate route open during data-plane failures.

**Why the others don't work:**
- In-band SSH: depends on production.
- Clientless VPN: depends on production.
- Jump box via VPN: depends on production.

skills: 3.5: Compare and contrast network access and management methods.
questions.question:
The security team wants all administrative SSH sessions to data-centre servers to traverse a single hardened gateway. Admins authenticate to this gateway, and from there they connect onward to individual servers. Direct SSH from analyst workstations to data-centre servers is blocked at the firewall.

Which design element is being described?

choices.text: A jump box (bastion host) that brokers administrative SSH sessions to internal hosts.
choices.explanation: Jump boxes are hardened intermediaries through which admin sessions are funnelled and logged.

choices.text: A clientless VPN portal publishing each server as a web application.
choices.explanation: Clientless portals publish web apps, not raw SSH session brokerage.

choices.text: A site-to-site VPN between the analyst workstations and the data centre.
choices.explanation: Site-to-site is gateway-to-gateway, not workstation-to-workstation.

choices.text: An out-of-band console server accessible only from the operations cell network.
choices.explanation: OOB consoles connect to device consoles, not user-to-server SSH brokerage.

questions.tip: Identify the hardened broker for administrative sessions.
questions.explanation:
A bastion or jump box is a single, controlled entry point for admin access.

**Why it works:** All SSH passes through the hardened gateway for control and logging.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Clientless portal: web-app publishing model.
- Site-to-site: network interconnect.
- OOB console: device-console focus.

skills: 3.5: Compare and contrast network access and management methods.
questions.question:
An automation team wants to manage a fleet of switches at scale, replacing manual web-UI changes with version-controlled configuration. They want one method that is suited to programmatic integration with their CI pipeline and another that remains the standard interactive shell for break-glass troubleshooting on a single device.

Which TWO methods should the team adopt for these purposes?

choices.text: REST API integration for programmatic configuration from the CI pipeline.
choices.explanation: REST APIs enable automated, scripted configuration at scale.

choices.text: SSH for interactive command-line troubleshooting on individual devices.
choices.explanation: SSH remains the standard secure interactive shell for break-glass access.

choices.text: Console-port access exclusively for both routine automation and troubleshooting.
choices.explanation: Console access does not scale to a fleet for routine automation.

choices.text: Vendor GUI screen-recording bots to replay clicks against the web UI.
choices.explanation: GUI screen-replay is fragile and not a recognised automation approach.

choices.text: Site-to-site VPN tunnels between every switch pair for in-band management.
choices.explanation: Switch-pair tunnels are not a management method for configuration delivery.

questions.tip: Pair an automation-friendly method with a standard interactive method.
questions.explanation:
An API supports automation at scale; SSH provides the interactive break-glass shell.

**Why it works:** Each fills the role described in the scenario.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Console only: not suited to bulk automation.
- GUI bots: fragile, not standard.
- Site-to-site VPN: not a management method.

skills: 3.5: Compare and contrast network access and management methods.
questions.question: Match each network access or management method to the scenario it best fits.

choices.text: Permanently interconnecting two branch offices at the firewall layer so subnets reach each other transparently
choices.explanation: Site-to-site VPNs interconnect networks at the gateway.

choices.text: Tunnelling all traffic from a remote employee laptop through corporate so web filtering applies to every flow
choices.explanation: A full-tunnel client-to-site VPN forces every flow through corporate.

choices.text: Funnelling all administrator SSH sessions through a single hardened broker before reaching internal servers
choices.explanation: Jump boxes are the canonical brokered-access pattern.

choices.text: Reaching a router's console through a cellular console server when the production link has failed
choices.explanation: OOB management provides an alternate path when production is down.

questions.tip: Match each method to whether it interconnects networks, secures a user session, or provides admin access.
questions.explanation: Each method maps to a distinct access or management need.

skills: 4.1: Explain the importance of basic network security concepts.
questions.question:
The operations team is rolling out centralized administrator authentication for a fleet of Cisco routers and switches. Auditors have asked that each individual command an engineer types at the CLI be authorized and logged separately from the login event itself, with the option to deny specific commands per role. The team must choose between two AAA protocols already supported on the platform.

Which protocol satisfies the auditor's requirement?

choices.text: TACACS+, because it separates authentication, authorization, and accounting and supports per-command authorization with full payload encryption.
choices.explanation: TACACS+ encrypts the entire packet and authorizes individual commands, which is why it is preferred for device administration.

choices.text: RADIUS, because it combines authentication and authorization in a single exchange and natively logs each typed command.
choices.explanation: RADIUS bundles authentication and authorization and only encrypts the password field, and it does not provide per-command authorization in the same way.

choices.text: LDAP simple bind, because the directory can store command privileges per user and the switch can query it at each keystroke.
choices.explanation: LDAP is a directory protocol, not an AAA protocol, and does not perform per-command authorization on network devices.

choices.text: SAML assertions, because they carry signed authorization attributes that the device can evaluate per CLI command.
choices.explanation: SAML is designed for browser-based federated SSO to web applications, not for CLI command authorization on routers and switches.

questions.tip: Think about which AAA protocol was designed specifically for managing access to network devices.
questions.explanation:
Centralized administration of routers and switches with per-command control is the canonical use case for TACACS+.

**Why it works:** TACACS+ separates the three AAA functions and lets the server return an authorization decision for each command entered, with the whole packet encrypted.

**Why the others don't work:**
- RADIUS: combines authn and authz, encrypts only the password, and is geared toward network access rather than device administration.
- LDAP simple bind: a directory lookup protocol, not AAA, and lacks command authorization semantics.
- SAML assertions: a federation standard for web SSO, not a CLI command gating mechanism.

skills: 4.1: Explain the importance of basic network security concepts.
questions.question:
During a compliance review, a hospital network team must justify protecting patient records on a SAN that already sits behind a firewalled VLAN with strict ACLs. The auditor argues that network controls alone do not prove the data is unreadable if a drive is removed from the array, walked out of the building, and connected to another host.

Which control directly addresses the auditor's concern?

choices.text: Enable full-disk or volume-level encryption on the SAN so that data at rest is unreadable without the storage encryption keys.
choices.explanation: Encrypting data at rest means a physically removed drive cannot be read without the key material held by the array.

choices.text: Force all client connections to the SAN over TLS so that any traffic captured between the host and the array is encrypted.
